meta.description: Yes, this is genuinely Goethe — from "From Makarie's Archive" in Wilhelm Meister's Journeyman Years (1829), not Bruce Lee, to whom it is now widely misattributed.

meta.ogDescription: Really Goethe, from Wilhelm Meister's Journeyman Years (1829) — not Bruce Lee, its most common modern misattribution.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Goethe line. It comes from “Aus Makariens Archiv” (“From Makarie’s Archive”), the set of aphorisms Goethe appended to Wilhelm Meisters Wanderjahre (Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years, complete edition 1829), and it also appears among his Maximen und Reflexionen. The German reads “Es ist nicht genug, zu wissen, man muß auch anwenden; es ist nicht genug, zu wollen, man muß auch tun.” The English shown is a faithful, widely-used translation, though the specific translator of this exact wording is not identified.

source.excerpt:
Es ist nicht genug, zu wissen, man muß auch anwenden; es ist nicht genug, zu wollen, man muß auch tun.

“Knowing is not enough; we must apply. Willing is not enough; we must do.”
trail: The German original — “Es ist nicht genug, zu wissen, man muß auch anwenden…” — is placed in “From Makarie’s Archive,” appended to Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years and later carried into the Maxims and Reflections, per Wikiquote’s sourced discussion.
Quotation databases pair the English line directly with Goethe’s German and the work title, e.g. buboquote.
Even where the line is filed under Goethe, it now carries a “misattributed-bruce-lee” tag, as on Goodreads.
source.excerptNote: The aphorism is one of many short reflections Goethe gathered under “From Makarie’s Archive” at the close of the novel.

Rights on the English line, however, follow whichever translation produced this exact wording — and that translator and edition are not identified, so no public-domain status can be asserted for the English text as shown.
source.useLine: Safe to credit to Goethe — this is a genuine aphorism from “Aus Makariens Archiv” in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years (1829). The German original is long in the public domain; the specific English translator of this exact wording is unidentified, so present the English as a standard translation rather than claiming public-domain status for the wording itself.

author.name: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
author.heading: About Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
author.bio: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was the towering figure of German letters, author of Faust, The Sorrows of Young Werther, and the two Wilhelm Meister novels. His late Wilhelm Meisters Wanderjahre (1829) closes with collections of aphorisms — including “From Makarie’s Archive” — where this maxim on turning knowledge and intention into action appears.

misattribution.heading: The mix-up
misattribution.intro: The words are Goethe’s, but online they are now most often stamped with a different name.

items.scope: Widely circulated on social media and quote sites
items.why: The martial artist admired and copied out lines like this, and motivational posts increasingly credit the phrase to him. Quote aggregators file it under Bruce Lee, and even Goethe-attributed listings now carry a “misattributed-bruce-lee” tag (Goodreads). There is no evidence Lee originated it.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Goethe’s, from “From Makarie’s Archive” in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years (1829), as documented on Wikiquote.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The maxim compresses a favourite Goethean theme — that insight and good intentions are inert until they issue in action. Its two-beat structure (know → apply, will → do) makes it endlessly quotable in self-improvement, business, and continuous-improvement contexts.
